conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because the postpartum weeks can bring big emotional shifts that are easy to overlook when you’re busy caring for a newborn.

Everything we discuss stays confidential between you and the clinical team; the goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can be honest about your experience. We’ll go through 10 questions about the past seven days, and I’ll ask them conversationally—no need to memorize any numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly? It’s been tough. I used to laugh so easily—little things my husband said or silly memes from friends—but lately it feels like I have to force it. Sometimes I’ll catch myself half-smiling when the baby does something cute, but the laughter just kind of fizzles out.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I guess I can still laugh, but it feels kind of distant—like I have to remind myself to do it. Nothing feels as funny as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep telling myself I *should* be excited about little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the baby for a walk—but when the moment comes, it feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I didn’t hold him long enough, or I’m just not cut out for this. Even when my partner says it’s normal newborn stuff, I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. My mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby—Is he breathing? Is that rash normal? Am I missing something?—even when nothing’s actually wrong. I’ll check on him every few minutes while he’s napping, and I can’t seem to shake the worry, even when everyone tells me he’s fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week my heart just started racing out of nowhere—like I’m suddenly convinced something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It’s that tight-chest, can’t-get-a-full-breath feeling. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

They really have. Some mornings I wake up already feeling behind—dishes piled, laundry everywhere, baby needing to be fed and changed—and it’s like I can’t see past the next hour. I’ll sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking I’ll never dig out, and my chest feels heavy. I still manage the basics, but it feels like I’m barely treading water most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby finally settles, I lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I think I did wrong that day, worrying about what tomorrow will bring. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and if I wake up for any reason, I can’t drift off again. I end up just staring at the ceiling feeling this heavy sadness.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason, or I’ll look at other moms on social media who seem so happy and think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” I keep telling myself I should be grateful, but the sadness is just… there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt like I must be doing everything wrong—I just sat in the rocker with tears streaming down while I tried to get him to latch. Another time my partner asked how my day was and I burst out crying before I could even answer.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for him.

It sounds as though the past week has felt heavy and overwhelming. You're working so hard to care for your baby, yet joy and laughter seem distant, replaced by a persistent gray cloud of sadness. Between constant self-blame, racing worry, sudden panic, and exhaustion from sleepless nights, it's understandable you feel you're barely treading water. I hear how much you love your little one and want to be there for him; reaching out for support now is a strong, caring step for both of you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges being able to laugh, but describes diminished enjoyment and effort required, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes an almost complete absence of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame (“I do that a lot”) and gives multiple examples of attributing baby’s fussing to personal failure, matching “Yes, most of the time.”</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attacks with racing heart, dread, and chest tightness occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to see past the next hour, and barely treading water—aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, severe sleep disruption due to racing thoughts and sadness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('most of the time'), tearfulness without cause, and social comparison distress—clearly aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 25/30 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>perinatal depression</med> with prominent <med>anxiety features</med>. You describe nearly constant <sym>sadness</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>, and multiple panic episodes meeting many <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Although you denied self-harm thoughts, the severity and functional impact warrant urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, support groups, and medication options compatible with breastfeeding if desired
3. Share these screening results and your full experience openly so your provider can develop a tailored care plan
4. Enlist trusted family or friends to help with household tasks, meals, or night shifts so you can rest
5. Practice brief self-compassion breaks: place a hand on your chest, breathe slowly, and remind yourself you're doing your best
6. Keep follow-up visits scheduled every 1-2 weeks until consistent improvement is seen
7. Maintain regular meals, hydration, and gentle outdoor time when possible; small steps count
8. If at any point you feel unable to stay safe with your baby, call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant < 1 mo  

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” frequent tearfulness  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia) in usual activities  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
- Chronic, intrusive “what-if” worries; motor tension with episodic panic (palpitations, chest tightness)  
- Difficulty initiating / maintaining sleep unrelated to infant needs  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “barely treading water,” daily functioning strained  

Risk pattern  
- Meets screening criteria for likely major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms; clinically significant distress and functional impairment present.  
- No self-harm ideation reported (denied on direct question).  

Next steps / referral  
- Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation; consider Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scoring and differential for postpartum depression, postpartum anxiety, and obsessive–compulsive or panic spectrum disorders.  
- Provide psychoeducation, support resources; schedule follow-up within one week to reassess mood, coping, and safety.
